lead: A dental X-ray machine is a small X-ray tube with a pointed cone. It makes one short exposure of a tooth onto film or a digital sensor. The tube has a fixed anode, a tungsten target and oil cooling. A step-up transformer gives the high voltage, and a timer switches it on for a set time. Dentists use it for periapical and bitewing views, and for panoramic imaging. Only a few universities teach this device in detail. Its design is a lesson in keeping dose low.
prereq: You need: basic X-ray production and the inverse-square law from a first-year physics course.

blocks.text: The tube is a stationary-anode type. A tungsten target sits in a vacuum glass envelope, and insulating oil around it carries heat away. Electrons from the filament hit the target and make X-rays. A step-up transformer raises the mains voltage to the tube voltage, set in kilovolt peak (kVp). The tube current, in milliamperes (mA), sets how many electrons flow. A timer closes the circuit for the exposure time in seconds (s). Dental units typically run at 60 to 70 kVp and 7 to 10 mA for 0.1 to 1 s, giving a few milliampere-seconds (mAs). Exposure quantity is mAs = mA × s. The timer must be accurate because a long exposure raises dose.

Inherent filtration comes from the tube wall and oil; added filtration is an aluminium sheet. Total filtration for a dental unit running at 70 kVp or below is at least 1.5 mm aluminium equivalent; units that work above 70 kVp need at least 2.5 mm aluminium. It removes soft X-rays that would only add skin dose. A collimator or lead diaphragm limits the beam to the cone opening. The cone, or position-indicating device, aims the beam at the tooth and sets the target-to-skin distance. A focal spot under 1 mm keeps the image sharp. Film speed or a digital sensor sets the dose needed for a good image.

blocks.where: I₁ and I₂ are beam intensities at distances d₁ and d₂ from the target; dose follows the same ratio.

blocks.text: An intra-oral periapical film shows the whole tooth and root apex. A bitewing shows crowns and crestal bone of upper and lower teeth in one bite. A panoramic unit (orthopantomogram, OPG) rotates a narrow beam and detector around the head to make one wide image of the jaws; it is not an intra-oral exposure. The operator stands at least 2 m away, behind a lead screen if possible, and wears a lead apron if staying in the room. A lead apron and thyroid collar protect the patient.

examples.question: A dental unit is set to 70 kVp, 7 mA and 0.6 s. (a) Find the exposure in mAs. (b) The cone is changed from 20 cm to 40 cm target-to-skin distance. By what factor does the skin dose change?
steps: Exposure: mAs = mA × s = 7 mA × 0.6 s = 4.2 mAs.
New skin dose = old dose / 4 = 0.25 of the old dose.
examples.answer: The exposure is 4.2 mAs, and the skin dose falls by a factor of 4 to one quarter of its old value.
examples.check:
mA = 7.0
t = 0.6
d1 = 20.0
d2 = 40.0
mas = mA * t
factor = (d2 / d1) ** 2
fraction = 1 / factor
print(mas)
print(factor)
print(fraction)

traps: kVp sets penetration and contrast; mA sets quantity. Do not use one for the other.
mAs = mA × s; mA alone is not exposure.
Doubling cone distance cuts dose by 4, not 2 (inverse square).
Timer is in seconds; 0.6 s is not 0.6 ms.

quiz.q: What kVp and mA range is typical for a dental unit?
quiz.a: About 60 to 70 kVp and 7 to 10 mA.

quiz.q: Why is the target made of tungsten?
quiz.a: Tungsten has a high atomic number and a high melting point, so it makes X-rays efficiently and survives heat.

quiz.q: A unit runs at 70 kVp, 7 mA and 0.6 s. Find the exposure in mAs.
The cone length goes from 20 cm to 30 cm. Find the factor by which skin dose changes.
quiz.a: (30/20)² = 2.25, so the new dose is 1/2.25 = 0.44 of the old dose.

quiz.q: What does added aluminium filtration do?
quiz.a: It removes low-energy X-rays that would only add skin dose.

quiz.q: Why does a digital sensor lower patient dose?
quiz.a: It needs fewer X-rays for the same image, so the required mAs and dose can be reduced.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) builds a 3D volume from many projections and is common in implant planning. Rectangular collimation and faster digital sensors cut dose further. Clinics audit dose and check timer accuracy as quality assurance. Search next: dental CBCT, aluminium equivalent filtration, position-indicating device.
